title: The Atomisation Payoff
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele reports on what adopting Atomisation, the lesson-design approach pioneered by Kris Boulton and championed by Craig Barton, has done for his planning and teaching. His central claim is that breaking a target problem into its constituent atoms both cuts planning time and raises lesson quality, because the single best explanation and example for each atom gets locked in. He sets out a 'double-win' of reusability: one atomised lesson serves every set he teaches, with lower sets spending longer on the basics and higher sets gaining time for extension, and it survives into the next academic year without a rebuild. He argues the saved time can be redirected to relationship-building and to rehearsing the script for each I Do. He then gives a four-step workflow (choose a multi-step example, break it into atoms, assess which atoms are secure, teach new atoms in isolation) and rebuts two misconceptions: that atomising adds work and that it makes teaching too slow. The piece ends by describing a Gemini Gem he built from his slide templates and past atomisations to automate the breakdown step.
points: Emanuele's reusability argument: an atomised lesson works across ability sets with little or no change to the slides, because only the time spent on each atom varies.
He claims Atomisation ends the 'these slides are terrible' problem by forcing the teacher to define one best explanation and example per atom, fixing instructional quality in place.
His starter workflow runs from a complex multi-step question down to its prerequisite atoms, checks which ones students already know, and teaches new atoms in isolation before chaining them.
He rebuts the objection that atomising slows lessons: spending two or three minutes on secure atoms frees time for the weak ones and prevents cognitive overload.
The AI section is presented as an accelerant, not the method: a Gemini Gem fed with his templates and past atomisations proposes atoms and prerequisite checks that he then refines.
quotes: Before Atomisation, I planned bespoke lessons, class-by-class, topic-by-topic. The result was hours of work for one single-use lesson.

The core atoms (I Do worked examples, We Do checks) are the same. For lower sets, the time spent practicing the basics is longer. For higher sets, their faster pace simply creates more time for high-level extension and challenge on the full chained process.

Because Atomisation forces you to define the single best, clearest explanation and example (the “atom”), the instructional quality is locked in. The lesson becomes structurally sound and easily reusable the following academic year, saving you the headache and time of a full rebuild.

Pre-Lesson Mastery: I can spend time thinking about the best way of teaching something and how to model a specific question—not what to put on the slide. This includes rehearsing the precise script for my I Do atom .

Actually, atomisation is a time-saver because it helps you identify and spend only 2–3 minutes on atoms students are already confident in. This precision avoids wasting time on mastered content and allows you to dedicate the majority of time and focus to the atoms where students are less confident.

Now, all I have to do is provide the learning objectives for a new lesson, and the system automatically performs the atomisation, suggesting the constituent atoms and the prerequisite checks. While the system is not perfect, it gives me loads of great starting ideas and structure, essentially automating the time-consuming breakdown process. I then just pick and refine the atoms I think will work best.
